title: Perfectionism and the pursuit of ideals
description: This article explores perfectionism, highlighting that while striving for high standards can be beneficial, it becomes harmful when it turns into rigid demands, leading to negative consequences like anxiety and life dissatisfaction. Real-life examples show how early experiences and upbringing can shape perfectionistic beliefs and behaviors. In conclusion, the author calls for a balance between striving for excellence and accepting reasonable results to avoid burnout and frustration.

texts: The desire to reach high standards, succeed in tasks, and be productive is actually a fairly positive quality.
It is similar to the desire to be accepted, approved, loved, or to achieve significant milestones in life.
When these remain at the level of desires, aspirations, or goals, we can call them adaptive beliefs that help us navigate life and keep us motivated.
But if these desires turn into rigid, fixed demands, and the cost of meeting them becomes too high, it is no longer just high standards—it is perfectionism.
What does it mean to be a perfectionist?
Perfectionism—the belief that everything must be performed 100% perfectly—is often at the root of many problems.
You strive for the ideal: mistakes are unacceptable, and failure feels like a catastrophe. You feel you must look, feel, think, and behave flawlessly in every situation.

As soon as you reach a goal, it is immediately replaced by a new, even more distant one, so you never truly enjoy or feel recognized for your efforts. Life becomes a gray, exhausting routine because you are constantly living to meet unrealistic and sometimes impossible standards.
In other words, a person with perfectionism:
• often compares themselves to others
• is in a state of permanent competition
• focuses on failures and setbacks while overlooking successes
• is harshly critical of themselves or others
• struggles to adapt to reality
• constantly procrastinates or puts things off
<q author="Elizabeth Gilbert">Perfectionism is fear in high heels and a fur coat, pretending to be elegant when, in reality, it is just scared.</q>
A model of perfectionism in practice

As a reminder, according to cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), our life experiences shape our beliefs about ourselves, others, and the world. These beliefs, in turn, determine our life strategies and rules.
Let’s look at Eugene as an example. His parents always held him to high standards; any grade below “excellent” was perceived as a failure.
Despite Eugene’s talent for music, his parents criticized his successes and pushed him toward a more “prestigious” career in medicine.
This experience formed a core belief in Eugene that he is “not good enough” and “incompetent.”
To compensate for this and feel capable and worthy, he developed a rule: “I must do everything perfectly.”

This drive for perfection forces Eugene to work to the point of exhaustion, scold himself for the slightest mistakes, and be overly critical of his colleagues. This leads to burnout, anxiety, relationship issues, and life dissatisfaction.
He often sets unrealistic goals, such as preparing a presentation perfectly within a very tight deadline.
If he succeeds (which is unlikely), his rule is reinforced, creating an illusion of control. If he fails, Eugene blames himself, strengthening his belief in his own incompetence.
This creates a vicious cycle: the rule “do everything perfectly” protects Eugene from the painful feeling of “not being enough,” but only as long as he can meet his inflated, unrealistic standards.
Any mistake triggers negative emotions, which intensifies self-criticism and fuels perfectionism.
What do perfectionistic beliefs sound like?
• I must do everything perfectly
• I must succeed at everything
• If I can’t give it my all, I might as well not do it at all
• If I’m being criticized, it means I’m doing a bad job. And I can’t do a bad job
• I don’t have the right to make mistakes
• I must be the best at everything I do
How is this constant drive for perfection formed?
Most often, this drive is formed during preschool or early school years as a result of family upbringing.
Researchers believe that neurotic perfectionism is shaped by childhood experiences with parents who showed love conditionally (based on grades, achievements, etc.) or provided no approval at all.

In both cases, a child develops a desire to be perfect to prove to their parents that they are worthy—both to themselves and to their parents. Often, perfectionist parents are overly critical, withhold support, and are highly demanding.
To meet their parents’ expectations and avoid punishment or criticism, a child feels they must strive for flawlessness.
There are four main parental behaviors that can contribute to the development of perfectionism:
• Parents themselves model perfectionistic behavior
• Parents are overly critical and demanding, lacking emotional support and guidance
• Parental approval is absent, inconsistent, or conditional
• An authoritarian parenting style and excessive parental expectations
Starting school encourages a child to formalize their achievements through grades.
This is where “overachiever syndrome” forms, which psychologists link to perfectionism. The child tries to be the best at everything, and if they fail, they fall into all-or-nothing thinking.
If they feel they can’t be the best in a subject, they may adopt a strategy of being the worst—thinking it’s better to be last if they can’t be first.
Beyond family influence, perfectionism is encouraged by modern society. In schools and universities, teachers favor compliant, high-achieving students, and employers value perfectionist employees.
The market economy pushes people toward competition and a constant drive to achieve better results.

The media dictates trends and our understanding of beauty and attractiveness. Looking good, dressing stylishly, and taking care of oneself can increase the chances of finding a partner, a prestigious job, or attractive friends.
Because of this, people often feel convinced that they must meet high standards to fit into society.
So, is perfectionism good or bad?
The question of perfectionism often sparks debate: some see it as useful, while others see it as harmful.

If you are a perfectionist, you might say that striving for excellence is normal—otherwise, how can you succeed? However, in practice, it drains your energy and resources, gradually but ruthlessly exhausting both your body and mind.
Perfectionism is closely linked to achievement addiction, which we discussed in previous chapters, so its drawbacks are similar.
Unrealistic, inflated standards affect almost every area of your life: work, studies, relationships, and even your downtime.
The problem is that the ideal perfectionism strives for is actually unattainable. An ideal doesn’t exist—it is a perceived state of perfection that everyone defines differently.
Let’s be honest and ask ourselves: is there anything that is absolutely perfect for everyone?
What you consider ideal might seem like nonsense to someone else. Even Mozart’s music and Da Vinci’s works aren’t for everyone, despite being considered masterpieces.
When you adjust your beliefs to align with reality, you can start to enjoy your work and life as a whole, rather than living in constant disappointment.
It is crucial to learn how to balance the drive for excellence with achieving acceptable, good results.

exercise.title: What to do when perfectionism feels overwhelming, perfection seems impossible, and you just want to live a normal life?
exercise.description: This article explores two types of perfectionism—negative and positive—and offers effective strategies for managing perfectionistic tendencies. We’ll cover eight key approaches, including finding motivation for change, cognitive restructuring, focusing on the process rather than the result, and forming new, healthier beliefs. The core idea is that you can overcome perfectionism by learning to embrace imperfection, practicing unconditional self-compassion, and prioritizing daily self-care.

texts: Modern researchers distinguish between two types of perfectionism: negative and positive—or, in other words, pathological and healthy.
To turn a disadvantage into an advantage, it’s important to balance your leadership qualities and drive for excellence with common sense and rationality.
We’ve prepared some effective recommendations to help you work through perfectionism.
The best starting point for tackling any problem is the motivation to change.
To overcome perfectionism, it’s important to understand why you want to change. Analyze and write down the pros and cons.
You might be surprised to find that the challenges far outweigh the benefits. Once you realize and accept this, change will become much easier.
Like many people, you might feel that everything must be done 100%, that making mistakes is unacceptable, or you may hold other similar perfectionistic thoughts and beliefs.
It is crucial to question these thoughts and work through them.
How? It helps to keep an automatic thought journal, where you can identify these ideas, test them against reality, and formulate a rational response.

<q author="Michael Jordan">I’ve missed more than 9,000 shots in my career. I’ve lost almost 300 games. 26 times, I’ve been trusted to take the game-winning shot and missed. I’ve failed over and over and over again in my life. And that is why I succeed.</q>
The following questions can help with reality testing (cognitive restructuring):
• What evidence do I have that supports this thought or belief?
• Is this thought helpful?
• Are there other ways I could think about this situation or myself?
• Am I blaming myself unnecessarily?
• What or who else contributed to this situation?
• Is this truly under my control?
• Am I holding myself to unreasonable or double standards?
• Is this a realistic expectation?
These questions are designed to test a belief—to confirm, clarify, or refute it—and to help you formulate an adaptive belief.

Ask yourself: if I do it perfectly, then what? And if I don’t do it perfectly, then what? Try to figure out what lies behind your perfectionism. Is it a fear of rejection? A fear of public ridicule? Or is there a craving for recognition hidden behind it?
Once you understand what lies behind your perfectionism, ask yourself: is this actually helping you address those fears and needs?

So, you wrote a perfect report and submitted it—now what? Are you no longer afraid that people will turn away from you? You gave a perfect presentation and everyone applauded—is that enough, just the applause of a crowd of strangers?
Most likely, the answer is no. You reach perfection, feel a moment of bliss, and then you’re right back in the race.
Get rid of black-and-white thinking
Perfectionists often think in terms of “all or nothing,” “success or failure,” or “do it perfectly or don’t bother at all.”

This approach is unrealistic. Look around and ask yourself: how many things in the world fit into the “all or nothing” category? Are your walls perfectly clean? Or is there at least a little bit of dust on them?
Do you know anyone who is absolutely calm and self-assured? Does your favorite actress possess perfect beauty, or does she have flaws too?
Life rarely comes without mistakes and setbacks.
No one is born a master—we learn, try, make mistakes, and gradually improve.

So, allow yourself to be imperfect, to do things incompletely, and to make mistakes. Errors aren’t enemies; they are helpers on your path to success. Remember the saying: “Only those who do nothing make no mistakes.”
Don’t try to abandon all your ideals at once—that might feel like too drastic a change.
Take it one step at a time.
Start small: pick one minor ideal and try to let it go. Observe the result.
The world won’t fall apart if you do something imperfectly. Your loved ones won’t turn away from you, and you won’t become a bad person.
You’ll likely find that handling an imperfect result is much easier than it seems. Remember, one experiment doesn’t give the full picture. You need to be consistent.
Every week or month, let go of one ideal and observe the reaction. Listen to yourself and move at a pace that feels comfortable for you.
Keep an achievement journal

Record both big and small successes, whether significant or not. Do this every day. Perfectionism thrives on failure; when you next tell yourself, “I never get anything right,” immediately open your journal and read how much you’ve actually accomplished.
Another way to overcome perfectionism is to focus on the process.
This means that when evaluating an action, you concentrate on the process rather than the result.

Imagine you’re a driver commuting from point A to point B every day. Some days, the lights are mostly green, and you reach your destination quickly. Other days, you hit constant red lights and get stuck in traffic, making the trip take much longer.
Your driving skills haven’t changed, so why not feel equally satisfied with the work you do every day? Try to look at things differently by not trying to make every task or action perfect.
For example, as a student, you could set process-oriented goals such as:
• attending classes;
• listening attentively and taking notes;
• asking relevant questions;
• dedicating a specific amount of time to each subject;
• reviewing your class notes every two to three weeks.
You can control all these processes, so success is guaranteed. In contrast, the final grade or result is not within your control.
The outcome depends on how your teacher feels that day, how well other students performed, what criteria they apply, and so on.
Try the “greed technique”
It’s based on a simple fact: most of us strive for perfection to succeed. It might not have occurred to you that you could be much more successful if you lowered your standards.
For example, a well-known psychotherapist once spent over two years writing his first scientific paper.

It was excellent and it was published. But in that same time, his colleagues had written and published significantly more works of similar quality. This made him wonder: what is better—having one paper that is 98% “perfect,” or 10 papers that are 80% “perfect”?
In the second case, his productivity would have been higher, and he might have gotten ahead of his colleagues. This realization prompted the psychotherapist to soften his standards.
As a result, his productivity increased, and his job satisfaction grew.
Completing several tasks well can be more effective than obsessing over a perfect product at the cost of high stress.
Formulate new beliefs
Working on beliefs involves recognizing them, reflecting on their consequences, finding their sources, and formulating new, adaptive beliefs.
Essentially, our goal is to help you “normalize” various forms of imperfection (like mistakes or slips) and help you accept the idea that both you and others are imperfect.
Abandon these beliefs:
• I/others/the world must be perfect
• If it’s not perfect, it’s bad
• If it’s bad, people will turn away from me / I won’t be recognized / I won’t cope
Instead, use these new beliefs and phrases:
I am not perfect, but I am:
• Learning and growing
• Good enough
• Deserving of love and respect, even if I’m not perfect
Others are not perfect, but they:
• Are also human, with their own strengths and flaws
• Won’t always approve of me, and that’s okay
I make mistakes, but they give me the chance to:
• Learn from them
• Become better
• Show resilience and keep going
Write down your new beliefs and integrate them into your life.
You can write them on a sticky note for your fridge, add them to your phone notes, or even create an image to use as your wallpaper.
Read these statements every day—at least once, but ideally more. This will help you reprogram your thoughts and replace unhelpful beliefs with more adaptive ones.
Fortunately, perfectionism is not a life sentence.
Through small steps—either on your own or with a psychologist—you can bring perfectionism down to a healthy level. To do this, learn to love yourself unconditionally and practice daily self-care.
